1 │ # Fields with underscores can only be set by typing the underscore
   2 │ 
   3 │ ## What happens now
   4 │ When I declare a field whose name has a leading or a trailing underscore, the setup method that the library writes for me accepts only the name with the underscores still attached. So every time I build the object, I have to type the underscore in the keyword myself.
   5 │ 
   6 │ ## What should happen
   7 │ I should be able to pass the value under the plain name, with the surrounding underscores left off, whether they sit at the start of the field name, at the end, or at both ends. The field on the object should still carry its full underscored name, and the printed form should still show the underscores.
   8 │ 
   9 │ ## About this project
  10 │ This is a small library for Python that writes simple data classes for you. You list your fields on a few lines, and the library gives you a setup method, a readable printed form, comparisons, and value checks, so you do not write that repetitive code by hand.
  11 │ 
  12 │ ## Problem this solves
  13 │ Today every place that creates the object has to repeat the underscores, which is noisy and easy to slip up on. Letting me drop them at the call site makes building the object read like ordinary code and keeps the naming of my fields to one place.
  14 │ 
  15 │ ## What changed
  16 │ The setup method the library writes now takes each field under the name with leading and trailing underscores removed. Fields that have a plain value, a made-on-demand value, or a value check are all set through that same short name. Nothing was taken away: the stored field and the printed form keep the underscored name, and field names written without any underscores behave exactly as they did before.
  17 │ 
  18 │ ## Impact
  19 │ Ease of use at the call site. Stored values and printed output stay the same, and existing field names without underscores are untouched.
  20 │ 
  21 │ ## User experience
  22 │ Before: I declare a field whose name starts with an underscore, and the only way to build the object is to pass the same underscored keyword, so every call site carries the underscore along. After: I pass the plain short name when I build the object, the value lands on the underscored field, and the object still prints with its underscored name.

+If you want to hide an attribute from the public API, you can prefix its name
+with an underscore.
+The underscore is just a convention to mark the attribute as private, so
+``attrs`` drops it from the argument name of the generated ``__init__`` and you
+can pass the plain name.
+The attribute itself and the ``repr`` keep the underscores:
+
+.. doctest::
+
+   >>> @attr.s
+   ... class SecretCoordinates(object):
+   ...     _x = attr.ib()
+   ...     _y = attr.ib()
+   >>> SecretCoordinates(1, 2)
+   SecretCoordinates(_x=1, _y=2)
+   >>> SecretCoordinates(x=1, y=2)
+   SecretCoordinates(_x=1, _y=2)
+
+
 Sometimes you want to have default values for your initializer.
 And sometimes you even want mutable objects as default values (ever used accidentally ``def f(arg=[])``?).

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

from __future__ import absolute_import, division, print_function

import pytest

import attr

from attr._make import Attribute, NOTHING

from . import TYPE


@attr.s
class C1(object):
    x = attr.ib(validator=attr.validators.instance_of(int))
    y = attr.ib()


foo = None


@attr.s()
class C2(object):
    x = attr.ib(default_value=foo)
    y = attr.ib(default_factory=list)


class TestDarkMagic(object):
    """
    Integration tests.
    """
    def test_ls(self):
        """
        `attr.ls` works.
        """
        assert [
            Attribute(name="x", default_value=None, default_factory=NOTHING,
                      validator=None),
            Attribute(name="y", default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=list,
                      validator=None),
        ] == attr.ls(C2)

    def test_to_dict(self):
        """
        `attr.to_dict` works.
        """
        assert {
            "x": 1,
            "y": 2,
        } == attr.to_dict(C1(x=1, y=2))

    def test_validator(self):
        """
        `instance_of` raises `TypeError` on type mismatch.
        """
        with pytest.raises(TypeError) as e:
            C1("1", 2)
        assert (
            "'x' must be <{type} 'int'> (got '1' that is a <{type} "
            "'str'>).".format(type=TYPE),
            C1.x, int, "1",
        ) == e.value.args

    def test_renaming(self):
        """
        Private members are renamed but only in `__init__`.
        """
        @attr.s
        class C3(object):
            _x = attr.ib()

        assert "C3(_x=1)" == repr(C3(x=1))

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-

from __future__ import absolute_import, division, print_function


import sys


PY3 = sys.version_info[0] == 3
# TYPE is used in exceptions, repr(int) is differnt on Python 2 and 3.
TYPE = "class" if PY3 else "type"


def simple_attr(name):
    """
    Return an attribute with a name and no other bells and whistles.
    """
    from attr import Attribute
    from attr._dunders import NOTHING
    return Attribute(name=name, default_value=NOTHING, default_factory=NOTHING,
                     validator=None)

        class C(object):

                Attribute("a",
                          default_value=2,
                          default_factory=NOTHING,
                          validator=None,),

                          default_value="hallo",
                          default_factory=NOTHING,
                          validator=None,),

                          default_value=None,
                          default_factory=NOTHING,
                          validator=None,),
            ]

        C = _add_init(C)
        i = C()
        assert 2 == i.a
        assert "hallo" == i.b
        assert None is i.c

    def test_default_factory(self):
        """
        If a default factory is present, it's used as fallback.
        """
        class D(object):
            pass

        class C(object):
            __attrs_attrs__ = [
                Attribute("a",
                          default_value=NOTHING,
                          default_factory=list,
                          validator=None,),
                Attribute("b",
                          default_value=NOTHING,
                          default_factory=D,
                          validator=None,)
            ]
        C = _add_init(C)
        i = C()
        assert [] == i.a
        assert isinstance(i.b, D)

    def test_validator(self):
        """

        """
        class VException(Exception):
